 16038  
 16039      DHS has also observed a pattern of students immediately 
 16040  transferring schools or changing educational levels or programs of 
 16041  study upon their arrival in the United States. These students often use 
 16042  an admission letter and Form I-20 from a well-known school to increase 
 16043  their odds of obtaining a student visa and then immediately request a 
 16044  transfer to their intended school or program of study once they have 
 16045  gained admission to the United States. Some of the most egregious 
 16046  examples are those who apply to a 4-year university, which requires 
 16047  demonstration of sufficient English level skills for enrollment in 
 16048  classes through the passage of the Test of English as a Foreign 
 16049  Language test (commonly known as TOEFL), receive their visa based on 
 16050  their declared intention of attending a 4-year university, and then 
 16051  transfer to English language programs upon arrival. Other, more 
 16052  dangerous examples, include those foreign students who receive a visa 
 16053  based on their declared intention to study the humanities, but then 
 16054  transfer into sensitive programs such as nuclear science. A handful of 
 16055  those have been arrested for spying for China.\314\ The existing 
 16056  regulations are vulnerable to exploitation by aliens who threaten U.S. 
 16057  national security. This rule is designed to reduce this vulnerability. 
 16058  Since 2020, there have been over 13,000 F-1 students who transferred 
 16059  before the start of classes or within their first term, including over 
 16060  4,400 students transferring from a higher education to ELT program of 
 16061  study within their first
 16062  
 16063  [[Page 45104]]
 16064  
 16065  term or session of a program of study.\315\ The number of F-1 students 
 16066  who changed their educational levels within the first 60 days of their 
 16067  program is close to 8,400.\316\ While the number of students 
 16068  transferring or changing educational levels represents a small 
 16069  percentage of the total F-1 student population, these transfers are 
 16070  often promoted by third-party recruiters and other for-profit entities 
 16071  to allow aliens to use the student visa process to mask their intent in 
 16072  the United States or circumvent F-1 restrictions.\317\ In addition, 
 16073  school officials are often burdened with the administrative costs of 
 16074  processing SEVIS transfer requests from F-1 students who misrepresented 
 16075  their intentions of studying at their institution.

 16099      While there may be legitimate cases of students who wish to change 
 16100  their educational objective to gain knowledge at a lower or the same 
 16101  educational level, the traditional path of study typically progresses 
 16102  from a lower educational program to a higher one. The existing 
 16103  regulations present a model consistent with the majority of bona fide 
 16104  students who follow this traditional trajectory. The term ``full course 
 16105  of study'' as defined in the existing regulations requires that the 
 16106  program ``lead to the attainment of a specific educational or 
 16107  professional objective.'' \318\ Repeated changes to a program of study 
 16108  either within the same educational level or to move to a lower level, 
 16109  as well as immediate changes to a program of study upon initial entry 
 16110  into the United States, are not consistent with attainment of such an 
 16111  educational or professional objective. This understanding was reflected 
 16112  in the preamble to a 1986 rulemaking proposing changes to the F 
 16113  regulations, which stated: ``The proposed regulation. . .places 
 16114  limitations on the length of time a student may remain in any one level 
 16115  of study. Thus, the Service has eliminated applications for [EOS] for 
 16116  students who are progressing from one educational level to another but 
 16117  has placed a control over students who, for an inordinate length of 
 16118  time, remain in one level of study.'' \319\ But, by 1991, INS 
 16119  eliminated all EOS applications and began to rely on DSO's to make the 
 16120  decision on whether educational progress was being made. In the decades 
 16121  that have followed, it has become clear that this has enabled thousands 
 16122  to stay here for decades by switching programs and not making any 
 16123  upward progress.\320\

 16144  214.2(f)(5)(ii)(A) and new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i). DHS believes these

 16156  nonimmigrant at one educational level will be unable to maintain F-1 
 16157  status, depart and be admitted in F-1 status, or otherwise obtain F-1

 16160  214.2(f)(5)(ii)(C). However, an F-1 student who has completed a program 
 16161  in the United States at one educational level and is beginning a new 
 16162  program at a higher educational level will be considered to be 
 16163  maintaining F-1 status if they otherwise comply with requirements under 
 16164  8 CFR 214.2(f). See new 8 CFR 214.2 (f)(5)(ii)(B). These provisions 
 16165  were retained from the NPRM to the final rule. They will be applied 
 16166  prospectively. Any programs completed prior to the effective date of 
 16167  the rule will not be counted towards the limits.\321\

 16169  
 16170      \321\ For example, an F-1 student who completed a master's 
 16171  degree prior to the effective date of the rule would be eligible to 
 16172  enroll in and be admitted for the completion of another master's 
 16173  degree. Any programs completed after the effective date of the rule 
 16174  would be counted towards the new limits of this rule.

 16176  
 16177      DHS believes that it is reasonable for a student to progress to a 
 16178  higher educational level rather than continue at the same level or 
 16179  pursue a lower level of education, as that is the traditional 
 16180  trajectory in the pursuit of higher education. Movement within the same 
 16181  level after completion of a program to a lower educational level raises 
 16182  concerns regarding whether the F-1 student is a bona fide student who 
 16183  intends to temporarily and solely pursue a full course of study rather 
 16184  than pursuing different degrees as a de facto way to prolong their stay 
 16185  in the United States.
 16186      If an F-1 student who has completed their first academic year of a 
 16187  program of study seeks to change educational objectives and this change 
 16188  would require an EOS, the alien would then apply for EOS using the form 
 16189  designated by USCIS, paying the required fee and following all form 
 16190  instructions, including submitting any biometrics required by 8 CFR 
 16191  103.16. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(D).
 16192      DHS recognized that these changes might require updates to SEVIS 
 16193  and other systems. Because the timeframe for those updates is not fixed 
 16194  and there could be technical issues regarding implementation, DHS is 
 16195  including a provision whereby DHS may delay or suspend implementation, 
 16196  in its discretion, if it determines that the change in educational 
 16197  level limitation is inoperable for any reason. The need for this 
 16198  provision is not indefinite and therefore DHS has added language in the 
 16199  regulatory text to clarify that this provision can be used for up to 
 16200  two years from the effective date of the rule (i.e., September 14, 
 16201  2028). See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(E). If DHS delays or suspends the 
 16202  provisions in this section governing the change in educational 
 16203  objectives, DHS will make an

 16205  [[Page 45105]]
 16206  
 16207  announcement of the delay or suspension by notice in the Federal 
 16208  Register and to the academic community through SEVP's various 
 16209  communication channels, including ICE.gov/sevis, Study in the States 
 16210  (https://studyinthestates.dhs.gov), and SEVIS Broadcast Message. DHS 
 16211  will also announce the implementation dates of the change in degree 
 16212  level provision through SEVP's communication channels (ICE.gov/sevis, 
 16213  Study in the States, and SEVIS Broadcast Message) at least 30 calendar 
 16214  days in advance.

 16216  respect to a change in level as DHS believes it accurately reflects 
 16217  current academic models. Specifically, ``educational'' captures 
 16218  programs for non-degree students, whereas using a term such as 
 16219  ``degree'' may not. For example, an F-1 student currently will not 
 16220  qualify for additional post-completion OPT if he or she changes to a 
 16221  non-degree certificate program, given that the certificate program is 
 16222  not a ``higher educational level.'' Similarly, certificate programs for 
 16223  professional advancement are typically not considered to be a ``higher 
 16224  educational level'' allowing students to qualify for additional post-
 16225  completion OPT.

 16227  the programs of study for which they were admitted to the United States 
 16228  and to only pursue additional programs of study that demonstrate an 
 16229  upward progression in degree levels, which is expected from a qualified 
 16230  bona fide student who is coming to the United States temporarily and 
 16231  solely to pursue a course of study. DHS believes that this restriction 
 16232  will not significantly impact the choice of bona fide students who come 
 16233  to the United States temporarily to complete a full course of study. 
 16234  The F-1 program, with its statutory requirement that an alien be a bona 
 16235  fide student who seeks to enter the United States temporarily and 
 16236  solely for the purpose of pursuing a full course of study at the school 
 16237  listed on his or her Form I-20 or successor form, should not be used by 
 16238  aliens wishing to remain in the United States indefinitely. These 
 16239  changes will better ensure that this statutory intent is fulfilled 
 16240  without hindering the options presented to bona fide students seeking 
 16241  study at higher educational levels and thus create a balanced solution 
 16242  to this issue.
 16243  3. Preparation for Departure
 16244      DHS retains its proposal from the NPRM to change the departure 
 16245  period for F nonimmigrants from 60 to 30 days. See new 8 CFR 
 16246  214.2(f)(5)(v). DHS received comments on this change, and those 
 16247  comments are discussed elsewhere in this preamble. DHS made this change 
 16248  for several reasons as discussed in the NPRM. The 60 days previously 
 16249  provided to F-1s to prepare for departure was twice as long as that of 
 16250  other SEVP programs (M and J nonimmigrants). See new 8 CFR 
 16251  214.2(j)(1)(ii) and 8 CFR 214.2(m)(10)(i). In addition, this 60-day 
 16252  period is also six times longer than certain nonimmigrants who are 
 16253  authorized to remain in the United States for years but are only 
 16254  provided with a 10-day period to depart the United States.
 16255      As discussed within the NPRM, DHS believes that 30 days for the F 
 16256  nonimmigrant population is the appropriate balance between a 60-day and 
 16257  a 10-day period of departure and has retained the proposed 30-day 
 16258  departure period for F-1 nonimmigrants in the final rule.\322\ 
 16259  Similarly, DHS notes that seeking an EOS or change of status is an 
 16260  allowable activity for F-1 nonimmigrants during the 30-day departure 
 16261  period following the completion of their program and incorporated this 
 16262  clarification in the proposed rule and retains it in the final rule. 
 16263  See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v).

 16377  days (which DHS is proposing to change to 30 days) to take the steps 
 16378  necessary to maintain legal status or depart the United States. See new 
 16379  8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v). However, because the change to H-1B status cannot 
 16380  occur until October 1, an F-1 student whose program or post-completion 
 16381  OPT expires in mid-spring has two or more months following the 60-day 
 16382  period before the authorized period of H-1B status can commence. To 
 16383  address this situation, commonly known as the ``cap-gap,'' DHS 
 16384  established regulations that automatically extended F-1 D/S and, if 
 16385  applicable, post-completion OPT employment authorization for certain F-
 16386  1 nonimmigrants until April 1 of the fiscal year for which the H-1B 
 16387  status is being requested or until the validity start date of the 
 16388  approved petition, whichever is earlier. See redesignated 8 CFR 
 16389  214.2(f)(5)(vii). The extension of F-1 D/S and OPT employment 
 16390  authorization is commonly known as the ``cap-gap extension.'' This rule 
 16391  does not change the ``cap-gap extension'' provisions; it simply removes 
 16392  the reference to D/S and makes clear that an automatic extension will 
 16393  be granted to those with a fixed period of stay.
 16394  b. F-1 Status and Authorized Employment While EOS and/or Employment 
 16395  Authorization Applications Are Pending
 16396      DHS struck ``duration of status'' from redesignated 8 CFR 
 16397  214.2(f)(5)(vii) in the proposed rule and clarified that an alien with 
 16398  F-1 status whose admission period as indicated on his or her I-94 has 
 16399  expired, but who has timely filed an EOS application, will be 
 16400  authorized to continue pursuing a full course of study after the end 
 16401  date of his or her admission until USCIS adjudicates the EOS 
 16402  application. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii). This change allows for 
 16403  ongoing authorization to continue studies as long as the student has 
 16404  timely filed his or her EOS and will not penalize students if USCIS is 
 16405  unable to adjudicate an EOS application before a student's new term or 
 16406  course of study is underway. In such cases, students will be able to 
 16407  continue pursuing their full course of study.\325\ This change is 
 16408  retained in the final rule.
 16409  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16410  
 16411      \325\ However, if the extension of stay application is received 
 16412  during the 30-day period under new paragraph 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v), 
 16413  the F-1 student is authorized to continue a full course of study but 
 16414  may not continue or begin engaging in practical training or other 
 16415  employment. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B).
 16416  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16417  
 16418      DHS did clarify the title of new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii) in the 
 16419  final rule, since the automatic extension is for the authorized period 
 16420  of stay while the EOS is adjudicated, rather than an automatic EOS. The 
 16421  title changed from ``Automatic Extension of F stay and employment 
 16422  authorization. . .'' to ``Automatic extension of the authorized period 
 16423  of stay and employment authorization. . .''
 16424      The shift to a fixed date of admission has implications for various 
 16425  types of employment authorization. Prior to the effective date of this 
 16426  final rule, DSOs could authorize certain types of employment 
 16427  authorization, including on-campus employment and CPT,\326\ and 
 16428  students generally did not need to be concerned about a specific 
 16429  expiration date for their student status, and thus their employment 
 16430  authorization, because they were admitted for D/S. This rule changes 
 16431  that framework with different implications for various types of 
 16432  employment authorization.
 16433  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16434  
 16435      \326\ See 8 CFR 214.2(f)(9)-(12), 8 CFR 274a.12(b)(6)(iv).
 16436  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16437  
 16438      For on-campus employment where no EAD is needed, DHS is allowing 
 16439  aliens in F-1 status to continue to be authorized for on-campus 
 16440  employment while their EOS applications with USCIS are pending, not to 
 16441  exceed a period of 240 days.\327\ See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii). If 
 16442  the EOS application is still pending after 240 days have passed, the F-
 16443  1 student will no longer be authorized for employment and will need to 
 16444  stop engaging in on-campus employment. DHS is allowing a 240-day 
 16445  automatic extension period in order to minimize disruptions to on-
 16446  campus employment by teaching assistants, post-graduates working on 
 16447  research projects, and other positions that are integral to an F-1 
 16448  student's educational program. Note that the 240 days start after the 
 16449  expiration of one's current stay. DHS has always encouraged and will 
 16450  continue to encourage all nonimmigrants to apply for EOS within
 16451  
 16452  [[Page 45107]]
 16453  
 16454  the six months \328\ preceding the expiration of their current 
 16455  authorized stay thereby providing an additional buffer against any 
 16456  disruption of the ability to work.
 16457  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16458  
 16459      \327\ See 8 CFR 214.2(f)(9)(i) for a description of on-campus 
 16460  employment. For on-campus employment that is based on severe 
 16461  economic hardship resulting from emergent circumstances pursuant to 
 16462  redesignated 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(vi), see later discussion for 
 16463  additional restrictions. The EOS application must be timely filed 
 16464  pursuant to the new paragraph at 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B). 
 16465  Moreover, if an F-1 student files an extension of stay application 
 16466  during the 30-day period provided in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v)(new), he 
 16467  or she does not receive an automatic extension of authorized 
 16468  employment, including on-campus, CPT, and severe economic hardship, 
 16469  and must wait for approval of the extension of stay application (and 
 16470  employment authorization application, if required) before engaging 
 16471  in CPT or employment. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii).
 16472      \328\ With respect to the earliest filing date for a Form I-539, 
 16473  there is no prohibition on filing the form before a certain date 
 16474  ahead of expiration.
 16475  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16476  
 16477      Likewise, DHS is allowing an automatic extension of off-campus 
 16478  employment authorization for up to 240-days during the pendency of the 
 16479  EOS application, for F-1 students who have demonstrated severe economic 
 16480  hardship pursuant to 8 CFR 214.2(f)(9)(ii)(C) and previously received 
 16481  an EAD from USCIS that expired at the program end date that is now 
 16482  being extended with the EOS application. See new 8 CFR 
 16483  214.2(f)(5)(viii). These circumstances may include loss of financial 
 16484  aid or on-campus employment without fault on the part of the student, 
 16485  substantial fluctuations in the value of currency or exchange rate, 
 16486  inordinate increases in tuition and/or living costs, unexpected changes 
 16487  in the financial condition of the student's source of support, medical 
 16488  bills, or other substantial and unexpected expenses. In such cases, DHS 
 16489  believes a 240-day automatic extension of employment authorization will 
 16490  help alleviate the severe economic hardship and avoid a disruption in 
 16491  their employment, especially given the fact that an EAD is required and 
 16492  the frequency at which these students must submit an application for 
 16493  employment authorization.\329\ Additionally, given that USCIS's average 
 16494  EAD processing time is typically 60-120 days for foreign students and 
 16495  90-120 for most others, a 240-day timeframe provides sufficient 
 16496  flexibility in case of unexpected delays.
 16497  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16498  
 16499      \329\ See 8 CFR 274a.12(c)(3). 8 CFR 214.2(f)(9)(ii)(F)(2) 
 16500  provides that employment authorization based upon severe economic 
 16501  hardship may be granted in one-year intervals up to the expected 
 16502  date of completion of the student's current course of study.
 16503  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16504  
 16505      For F-1 students granted off-campus employment authorization on the 
 16506  basis of severe economic hardship resulting from emergent circumstances 
 16507  pursuant to redesignated 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(vi), DHS proposed, and is 
 16508  retaining in the final rule, an automatic extension of such employment 
 16509  authorization with a different validity period than the general 8 CFR 
 16510  214.2(f)(9)(ii)(C) severe economic hardship employment authorization 
 16511  extension described above while their EOS applications are pending. See 
 16512  new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii). This will codify USCIS's current policy 
 16513  which states USCIS may grant SSR employment authorization for the 
 16514  duration of the Federal Register notice validity period, but the period 
 16515  of authorization may not exceed the F-1 student's academic program end 
 16516  date.\330\
 16517  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16518  
 16519      \330\ See generally USCIS Policy Manual, Vol. 2, Part F, Chap. 
 16520  6, Employment, https://www.uscis.gov/policy-manual/volume-2-part-f-chapter-6 (last visited Feb. 4, 2026).
 16521  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16522  
 16523      As first promulgated in 1998, the SSR regulations provide necessary 
 16524  flexibility to address unforeseeable emergencies by allowing DHS, by 
 16525  notice in the Federal Register, to suspend the applicability of some or 
 16526  all of the requirements for on- and off-campus employment authorization 
 16527  for specified F-1 students where an emergency situation has arisen 
 16528  calling for this action. These F-1 students must continue to attend 
 16529  classes but are allowed to take a reduced course load. By regulation, 
 16530  aliens approved for SSR to take at least 6 semester or quarter hours of 
 16531  instruction at the undergraduate level or 3 semester or quarter hours 
 16532  of instruction at the graduate level. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v). 
 16533  Failure to take the required credits could be considered a failure to 
 16534  maintain F-1 status. The SSR regulations are announced by notice in the 
 16535  Federal Register, and such employment may only be undertaken during the 
 16536  validity period of the SSR notice.
 16537      Due to the shift to a fixed admission period, DHS proposed to 
 16538  provide an automatic extension of SSR-based employment so aliens' 
 16539  ability to benefit from this long-standing regulatory relief is not 
 16540  interrupted by USCIS processing times. This change is consistent with 
 16541  current USCIS policy, which allows for SSR employment authorization to 
 16542  be granted for the duration of the Federal Register notice validity 
 16543  period, so long as the period of authorization may not exceed the F-1 
 16544  student's academic program end date. It is also consistent with 
 16545  existing practice for certain nonimmigrants who require an EAD.\331\ 
 16546  This is retained in the final rule. Further, DHS has retained its 
 16547  proposal to automatically extend SSR authorization if an F-1 student 
 16548  has a timely-filed EOS pending for up to the end date stated in the 
 16549  Federal Register notice announcing the suspension of certain 
 16550  requirements, or 240 days, whichever is earlier. See new 8 CFR 
 16551  214.2(f)(5)(viii).
 16552  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16553  
 16554      \331\ See 8 CFR 214.2(f)(10)-(12), 8 CFR 274a.12(b)(6)(iv).
 16555  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16556  
 16557      As evidence of these automatic extensions of employment 
 16558  authorization, DHS will allow the F-1 student's I-94 (or successor 
 16559  form) or EAD (Form I-766, or successor form), for F-1 nonimmigrants 
 16560  requiring an EAD, when combined with a notice issued by USCIS 
 16561  indicating receipt of a timely filed EOS application (such as the Form 
 16562  I-797),\332\ to be considered unexpired until USCIS issues a decision 
 16563  on the EOS application, not to exceed 240 days. See new 8 CFR 
 16564  214.2(f)(5)(viii). SSR-based employment authorization that has been 
 16565  automatically extended can be evidenced by the F-1 student's EAD and 
 16566  the receipt notice issued by USCIS (the Form I-797), not to exceed the 
 16567  lesser of 240 days or the end date stated in the Federal Register 
 16568  notice announcing the suspension of certain requirements.
 16569  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16570  
 16571      \332\ However, if an F-1 student files an extension of stay 
 16572  application during the 30-day period provided in new paragraph 8 CFR 
 16573  214.2(f)(5)(v), he or she does not receive an automatic extension of 
 16574  authorized employment, including on-campus, CPT, and severe economic 
 16575  hardship, and must wait for approval of the extension of stay 
 16576  application (and employment authorization application, if required) 
 16577  before engaging in CPT or employment. 214.2(f)(5)(viii).
 16578  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16579  
 16580  5. New Process for EOS Application
 16581      Under current regulations, F-1 students may obtain a program 
 16582  extension from a DSO as long as they are maintaining status and making 
 16583  normal progress toward the completion of their educational objectives. 
 16584  See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(i) and (iii). The problem with the ``normal 
 16585  progress'' standard is that it is undefined, and DHS believes that 
 16586  retaining it could lead to inconsistent adjudications. Even now, the 
 16587  lack of a standard definition for normal progress leads DSOs to 
 16588  inconsistently extend F-1 students' program end dates and thus their 
 16589  stay in the United States. Some DSOs use a strict standard, evaluating, 
 16590  for example, documentation to support a student's claim of a compelling 
 16591  medical condition or illness that serves as the basis for the student's 
 16592  request for extension of the student's current program. However, other 
 16593  DSOs claim that the student is making ``normal progress'' whenever a 
 16594  student simply needs more time to complete the program. This 
 16595  inconsistency results in some students being able to remain in F-1 
 16596  status for years simply by having the DSO update the Form I-20 without 
 16597  providing a justification as to how the student is making ``normal 
 16598  progress'' and what academic or medical circumstances necessitate the 
 16599  extension of the program.
 16600      Therefore, DHS proposed not to use a ``normal progress'' standard 
 16601  with respect to seeking a program extension, and to require, in 
 16602  addition to the requirement that the applicant obtain a Form I-20 from 
 16603  the DSO recommending extension of the program, the applicant will be 
 16604  required to file an EOS
 16605  
 16606  [[Page 45108]]
 16607  
 16608  application to request additional time to complete their current course 
 16609  of study beyond their authorized period of admission. See new 8 CFR 
 16610  214.2(f)(7)(i). This change is retained in the final rule.
 16611      Apart from pursuing a new course of study, DHS appreciates that the 
 16612  time for study can legitimately fluctuate given the changing goals and 
 16613  actions of the student. For example, a student may experience 
 16614  compelling academic or medical reasons, or circumstances beyond their 
 16615  control that cause them to need additional time in the United States 
 16616  beyond the predetermined end date of the program in which they were 
 16617  initially enrolled. DHS understands these circumstances arise and 
 16618  believes these scenarios present an appropriate situation for DHS to 
 16619  directly evaluate the nonimmigrant's eligibility for additional time in 
 16620  the United States. However, instead of effectively extending their stay 
 16621  through a DSO's program extension recommendation in SEVIS, students 
 16622  will have to obtain a Form I-20 from the DSO recommending a program 
 16623  extension and apply to USCIS for an EOS. Immigration officers thereby 
 16624  will be able to conduct appropriate background and security checks on 
 16625  the applicant at the time of the EOS application and directly review 
 16626  the proffered evidence to ensure that the alien is eligible for the 
 16627  requested EOS, including through assessing whether the alien remains 
 16628  admissible. See 8 CFR 214.1(a)(3)(i). This extra step is necessary 
 16629  because an immigration officer will be able to see a more fulsome 
 16630  picture while considering the student's particular circumstances, and 
 16631  be able to identify potential fraud and criminality, thereby ensuring 
 16632  public safety and program integrity.
 16633      In these circumstances, DHS will only extend the stay beyond the 
 16634  program end date of an otherwise eligible F-1 student requesting 
 16635  additional time to complete their program if the additional time needed 
 16636  is due to a compelling academic reason, documented medical illness or 
 16637  medical condition, or circumstance that was beyond the student's 
 16638  control. As with all nonimmigrant EOS requests, an alien seeking an EOS 
 16639  generally must have continually maintained status.\333\ If an F-1 
 16640  student dropped below a full course of study, that drop must have been 
 16641  properly authorized. F-1 students seeking extensions of stay must 
 16642  primarily be seeking to temporarily stay in the United States solely to 
 16643  pursue a full course of study, INA section 101(a)(15)(F)(i), 8 U.S.C. 
 16644  1101(a)(15)(F)(i), and not for other reasons separate from, or in 
 16645  addition to, pursuing a full course of study.
 16646  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16647  
 16648      \333\ Failure to file on or before the expiration of the 
 16649  previously accorded status or failure to maintain such status may be 
 16650  excused at the discretion of USCIS if the alien demonstrates that at 
 16651  the time of filing: the delay was due to extraordinary circumstances 
 16652  beyond the control of the applicant, and USCIS finds the delay 
 16653  commensurate with the circumstances, the alien has not otherwise 
 16654  violated his or her status, and is not subject to deportation. See 8 
 16655  CFR 214.1(c)(3)(viii).
 16656  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16657  
 16658      If an F-1 student were to violate the terms of his or her F-1 
 16659  status, the F-1 student would need to apply to USCIS for reinstatement, 
 16660  consistent with 8 CFR 214.2(f)(16). If a student is reinstated and his 
 16661  or her admit until date expires within 6 months, but the student is 
 16662  unable to complete his or her program of study within that time, then 
 16663  the F-1 student also would need to apply to USCIS for an EOS. In that 
 16664  scenario, the F-1 student would need to make separate requests for 
 16665  reinstatement and for EOS by submitting a separate form for each 
 16666  request, including the required filing fee for each form, by marking 
 16667  reinstatement on one form and then EOS on the other. Both forms can 
 16668  then be submitted together at the same time to avoid unnecessary 
 16669  adjudication delays. In the event both forms are submitted together, 
 16670  and the F-1 student's application to reinstate student status is 
 16671  denied, his or her application for EOS would also be denied, with both 
 16672  filing fees being retained by USCIS and not refunded.
 16673      By way of illustration, a student with a fixed date of admission 
 16674  may request an additional 4 months to complete his or her program 
 16675  because the student was authorized to drop below a full course of study 
 16676  for one semester due to illness. Prior to the effective date of this 
 16677  final rule, the student would need to request an updated Form I-20 from 
 16678  the DSO recommending a program extension. Now, consistent with the 
 16679  proposal in the NPRM, an immigration officer could review the proffered 
 16680  evidence and ensure that the claim is supported by documentation from a 
 16681  medical doctor. Conversely, a student may request an EOS for additional 
 16682  time to complete an associate program but fail to submit evidence they 
 16683  were properly authorized to drop below a full course of study. The 
 16684  immigration officer has discretion to request transcripts from the 
 16685  student. If a student's transcripts reflect that the student failed 
 16686  multiple classes one semester, an immigration officer could determine 
 16687  if the student has failed to maintain status due to a failure to carry 
 16688  a full course of study as required. In another example, a student could 
 16689  submit an EOS request to continue in the same program because he or she 
 16690  was unable to take all the required classes for his or her major due to 
 16691  over-enrollment at the school. Again, an officer could request 
 16692  additional information, if needed, to determine that the student was 
 16693  maintaining a full course of study (or, if not, was properly authorized 
 16694  to reduce his or her course load), but due to the school's high 
 16695  enrollment, the student may validly require an additional semester to 
 16696  complete the degree requirements in order to graduate.
 16697      Therefore, DHS proposed to eliminate a reference to ``normal 
 16698  progress'' with respect to seeking a program extension, and incorporate 
 16699  a new standard clarifying that acceptable reasons for requesting an 
 16700  extension of a stay for additional time to complete a program are: (1) 
 16701  compelling academic reasons; (2) a documented illness or medical 
 16702  condition; or (3) exceptional circumstances beyond the control of the 
 16703  alien. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(i)(C).\334\ These provisions are 
 16704  retained in the final rule.
 16705  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16706  
 16707      \334\ DHS did not propose to update the term ``normal progress'' 
 16708  as defined in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(6)(i)(E). The provision at 8 CFR 
 16709  214.2(f)(6)(i)(E) relates to study at an approved private elementary

 16714  
 16715      The first two factors are based on the current regulatory 
 16716  provisions for program extension, 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii), from the 2025 
 16717  text (e.g., changes of major or research topics, and unexpected 
 16718  research problems). DHS proposed to clarify that, in addition to 
 16719  academic probation and suspension, a student's repeated inability or 
 16720  unwillingness to complete his or her course of study, as demonstrated 
 16721  by a pattern of failing classes and requesting multiple program 
 16722  extension, is not an acceptable reason to request an EOS for additional 
 16723  time to complete a program. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(i)(C)(1). This is 
 16724  also retained in the final rule.
 16725      DHS expects bona fide students to be committed to their studies, 
 16726  attending classes as required, carrying a full course of study, and 
 16727  making reasonable efforts toward program completion. Repeatedly failing 
 16728  classes demonstrates that the student is not making reasonable efforts 
 16729  toward completing his or her program of study. Therefore, a student who 
 16730  has a pattern of failing classes that has resulted in multiple program 
 16731  extensions would not be qualified for an EOS. The prohibition against 
 16732  requesting an EOS would not include students, such as those who, 
 16733  pursuant to DHS regulations, are making normal progress toward 
 16734  completing their program of study and still may not complete the 
 16735  program within 4 years
 16736  
 16737  [[Page 45109]]
 16738  
 16739  due to the standard timeline and requirements for the program. Absent 
 16740  such factors as being placed on academic probation or suspension, or 
 16741  repeatedly failing classes, these students would be eligible for 
 16742  extension based upon compelling academic reasons. This prohibition also 
 16743  does not include cases where the DSO properly authorized the student to 
 16744  drop below a full course of study as well as cases in which the status 
 16745  has been reinstated following a loss of status. In such case, the 
 16746  student is eligible for reinstatement if the reduced course load was 
 16747  within the DSO's power to authorize. A student would be expected to 
 16748  provide evidence demonstrating the compelling academic reason in order 
 16749  for the DSO to recommend a program extension. The student may then 
 16750  apply for an EOS. While a letter from the student may be sufficient to 
 16751  meet his or her burden of proof, an immigration officer will evaluate 
 16752  the individual case and make the determination as to whether additional 
 16753  evidence (such as a letter from a member of the school administration 
 16754  or faculty) is needed to adjudicate the case.
 16755      DHS also proposed to clarify that a student can qualify for a 
 16756  program extension and corresponding EOS based on a documented illness 
 16757  or medical condition. To provide an objective standard, DHS proposed to 
 16758  codify standards already included in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(6)(iii)(B), which 
 16759  requires a student to provide medical documentation from a licensed 
 16760  medical doctor, licensed doctor of osteopathy, licensed psychologist, 
 16761  or licensed clinical psychologist to substantiate the illness or 
 16762  medical condition if seeking a reduced course load. See new 8 CFR 
 16763  214.2(f)(7)(i)(C)(2). This is retained in the final rule. As this is 
 16764  already a long-standing requirement for DSOs and students in a similar 
 16765  context, DHS believes this will be appropriate and easy to implement in 
 16766  the program extension and corresponding EOS process. Further, requiring 
 16767  applicants to provide documentation of their medical illness or medical 
 16768  condition that caused their program delay is a reasonable request, 
 16769  because they are asking DHS to provide them additional time in the 
 16770  United States.
 16771      DHS also proposed a new factor in the EOS provisions--circumstances 
 16772  beyond the student's control, including a natural disaster, a national 
 16773  health crisis, or the closure of an institution. See new 8 CFR 
 16774  214.2(f)(7)(i)(C)(2)(iii). This is retained in the final rule. As in 
 16775  the reinstatement context, DHS believes that there might be additional 
 16776  reasons beyond compelling academic or documented medical reasons that 
 16777  result in a student's inability to meet the program end date listed on 
 16778  the Form I-20.
 16779      Therefore, DHS proposed a third prong that encompasses scenarios 
 16780  that are not envisioned in the current provisions governing the 
 16781  extension of a program end date, such as those noted above. Some 
 16782  scenarios are currently in the reinstatement provisions, 8 CFR 
 16783  214.2(f)(16)(i)(F), such as natural disasters, pandemics, and the 
 16784  negligence of a DSO, and DHS believes that they merit favorable 
 16785  consideration in extension requests moving forward. Other scenarios may 
 16786  present circumstances that require a more intensive, fact-specific 
 16787  analysis and may fall into this proposed third prong. For example, the 
 16788  circumstances surrounding the closure of a school may be considered in 
 16789  determining whether the student qualifies for an EOS. By way of 
 16790  illustration, if a school closes as a result of a criminal conviction 
 16791  of its owners for engaging in student visa fraud by not requiring 
 16792  students to attend, but the student is unable to demonstrate that he or 
 16793  she was attending classes prior to closure as required to fulfill a 
 16794  full course of study, the closure of the institution might not qualify 
 16795  the student for a program extension. In contrast, if a school closes 
 16796  but a student is able to demonstrate that he or she was attending 
 16797  classes and was fulfilling all requirements to otherwise remain in 
 16798  status, the closure of the institute may qualify the student for a

 16811      Where the alien requests a recommendation to extend the program end 
 16812  date, the DSO could only make a recommendation to extend the program if 
 16813  the alien requested the extension before the program end date noted on 
 16814  the most recent Form I-20, or successor form. Additionally, consistent 
 16815  with changes throughout this rule, once the DSO recommends the 
 16816  extension of the program, the alien would need to timely file for an 
 16817  EOS on the form and in the manner designated by USCIS, with the 
 16818  required fees and in accordance with the filing instructions, including 
 16819  any biometrics required by 8 CFR 103.16 and a valid, properly endorsed 
 16820  Form I-20 or successor form, showing the new program end date barring 
 16821  extraordinary circumstances. See 8 CFR 214.1(c)(4) and new 8 CFR 
 16822  214.2(f)(7)(ii) and (f)(7)(iii). This is retained in the final rule.
 16823      If seeking an EOS to engage in any type of practical training, the 
 16824  alien in F-1 status will also need to have a valid Form I-20, properly 
 16825  endorsed for practical training, and be eligible to receive the 
 16826  specific type of practical training requested. See new 8 CFR 
 16827  214.2(f)(7)(v). This is retained in the final rule. Finally, as with 
 16828  all immigration benefit requests, an immigration officer will generally 
 16829  not grant an EOS where an alien in F-1 status failed to maintain his or 
 16830  her status.
 16831      Finally, a student's failure to timely request, from the DSO, a 
 16832  recommendation for extension of the program end date prior to 
 16833  expiration of the student's authorized stay, which would result in the 
 16834  DSO recommending an extension of the program end date in SEVIS after 
 16835  the end date noted on the most recent Form I-20 or successor form, will 
 16836  require the alien to file for a reinstatement of F-1 status, because 
 16837  the alien will have failed to maintain status and will be ineligible 
 16838  for an EOS. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(viii). A request for 
 16839  reinstatement must be filed in the manner and on the form designated by 
 16840  USCIS, with the required fee, including any biometrics required by 8 
 16841  CFR 103.16. DHS is also requiring F-2 dependents seeking to accompany 
 16842  the F-1 principal student to file applications for an EOS or 
 16843  reinstatement, as applicable. These requirements are consistent with 
 16844  current provisions.
 16845      With the transition from D/S to admission for a fixed time period, 
 16846  F-1 students will need to apply for an EOS directly with USCIS, by 
 16847  submitting the appropriate form and following the requirements outlined 
 16848  in the form instructions. USCIS anticipates accepting the Form I-539, 
 16849  Application to Change/Extend Nonimmigrant Status, for this population 
 16850  but would like the flexibility to use a new form if more efficient or 
 16851  responsive to workload needs. Thus, DHS is retaining its proposal to 
 16852  use general language to account for a possible change in form in
 16853

 16856  the future. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(A). If the form ever 
 16857  changes, USCIS would provide stakeholder's advance notice on its web 
 16858  page and comply with Paperwork Reduction Act requirements.
 16859      Like all other aliens who file a Form I-539, F-1 applicants may be 
 16860  required to submit biometrics and may be required to appear for an 
 16861  interview pursuant to 8 CFR 103.2(b)(9). In addition, applicants will 
 16862  need to demonstrate that they are eligible for the nonimmigrant 
 16863  classification sought. Accordingly, applicants must submit evidence of 
 16864  sufficient funds to cover expenses. A failure to provide such evidence 
 16865  will render the applicant ineligible for the EOS. See new 8 CFR 
 16866  214.2(f)(7)(ii).
 16867      While the sponsoring school is required to verify the availability 
 16868  of financial support before issuing the Form I-20, they may not be 
 16869  well-versed in foreign documentation submitted by applicants and 
 16870  circumstances may change between the issuance of a Form I-20 and a 
 16871  request for an EOS. Further, it is incumbent upon DHS to determine the 
 16872  veracity of the evidence submitted, and officers must ensure that the 
 16873  student has sufficient funds to study in the United States without 
 16874  resorting to unauthorized employment. The phrase ``sufficient funds to 
 16875  cover expenses'' is referred to in existing DoS regulations concerning 
 16876  issuance of F and M nonimmigrant student visas, 22 CFR 41.61(b)(1)(ii), 
 16877  and current DoS policy requires an applicant to provide documentary 
 16878  evidence that sufficient funds are, or will be, available to defray all 
 16879  expenses during the entire period of anticipated study.\335\ While this 
 16880  does not mean that the applicant must have cash immediately available 
 16881  to cover the entire period of intended study, which may last several 
 16882  years, the applicant must demonstrate enough readily available funds to 
 16883  meet all expenses for the first year of study and that additional funds 
 16884  will be available for the duration of the intended period of 
 16885  study.\336\ DHS believes requiring evidence of readily available 
 16886  financial resources to cover expenses for one year of study is 
 16887  reasonable given that F students are familiar with this requirement 
 16888  because this is the standard used by the DoS in the issuance of F 
 16889  nonimmigrant visas. DHS also considers that this standard is 
 16890  appropriate because it establishes concrete resources for one full

 16893  available for each subsequent year of study from the same source or 
 16894  from one or more other specifically identified and reliable financial 
 16895  sources. Such evidence for one year and subsequent years could include,

 16899  letter from the school accounts office indicating tuition payments 
 16900  already made and any outstanding account balance; affidavits of support 
 16901  from a sponsor; proof of authorized private student loans; \337\ and/or

 16987  6. School Transfers and Changes in Educational Objectives
 16988      The proposed rule discussed several examples of fraudulent ``pay-
 16989  to-stay'' schemes in which students were falsely reported as 
 16990  maintaining status in return for cash payments to DSOs.\339\ 
 16991  Furthermore, the D/S framework has enabled some aliens to become 
 16992  ``professional students'' who spend years enrolled in programs at the 
 16993  same educational level (for example, multiple associate degree 
 16994  programs) or complete programs at one educational level and enroll in 
 16995  lower educational levels (such as completing a master's degree and then 
 16996  enrolling in an associate program).\340\ While admission for a fixed 
 16997  time period will help to address these concerns, DHS proposed 
 16998  limitations on program changes within and between educational levels to 
 16999  further strengthen the integrity of the F nonimmigrant visa 
 17000  classification by better ensuring that aliens are in the United States 
 17001  primarily to study, rather than to reside permanently in the United 
 17002  States. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i). The final rule retains this 
 17003  provision.

 17012  change of educational level conditions. First, as is the case

 17016  Form I-20; and second, if the alien is authorized to engage in post-

 17019  recommended OPT or the date the OPT authorization ends, whichever is

 17021  NPRM, the regulatory text in the final rule replaces the statement that 
 17022  the F-1 student ``must be able to resume classes within 5 months. . .''

 17024  months . . .''. See new CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(G) and (H).
 17025      DHS retained the current provisions at 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i), 
 17026  rendering aliens who do not pursue a full course of study ineligible to 
 17027  change programs or transfer schools, and clarifying that failure to 
 17028  pursue a full course of study includes, but is not limited to, a 
 17029  student whose pattern of behavior demonstrates a repeated inability or 
 17030  unwillingness to complete his or her course of study. Just as delays 
 17031  caused by unacceptable patterns of behavior, academic probation or 
 17032  suspension are not acceptable reasons for program extensions and 
 17033  corresponding EOS of a student's current program, neither are they an 
 17034  acceptable reason for failing to carry a full course load. Such aliens 
 17035  will have failed to maintain F status, are ineligible for a change of

 17038      To complete a transfer, an F-1 student must first notify the 
 17039  student's current school (the ``transfer-out school'') of the intent to 
 17040  transfer and indicate the school to which the student intends to 
 17041  transfer (the ``transfer-in school''). Upon notification by the 
 17042  student, the transfer-out school will update the student's record in 
 17043  SEVIS as a ``transfer-out'' and indicate the transfer-in school and a 
 17044  release date. The release date will be the current semester or session 
 17045  completion date, or the date of expected transfer if earlier than the 
 17046  completion date of the established academic cycle. The transfer-out 
 17047  school will retain control over the student's record in SEVIS until the 
 17048  student completes the current term or reaches a release date, whichever 
 17049  is earlier. At the request of the student, the DSO of the current 
 17050  school may cancel the transfer request at any time prior to the release

 13420      Commenters stated that, under the proposed rule, many foreign 
 13421  students are likely to incur costs for at least one EOS application, 
 13422  with many needing to file multiple EOS applications due to changes in 
 13423  academic level or participation in OPT. One of these commenters 
 13424  referenced a common educational path, Bachelor's degree, OPT, Master's 
 13425  degree, OPT, and STEM OPT, which would require four separate EOS 
 13426  filings with USCIS and an approximate cost of $1,680.
 13427      Response: DHS acknowledges that EOS filings will incur costs to 
 13428  nonimmigrants. Table 16, Applicant Unit Costs for Filing an EOS with 
 13429  USCIS of the final Regulatory Impact Analysis calculates the various 
 13430  costs that could be assumed for an EOS request. These costs include 
 13431  assistance and differences in submission type. These costs would only 
 13432  be incurred if the nonimmigrant files an EOS request and would not be 
 13433  concurrent with fees such as the Visa Application Fee.
 13434      DHS acknowledges that some nonimmigrants will incur multiple EOS 
 13435  requests. These costs are not expected to occur in a single instance 
 13436  and would be dispersed across multiple years according to the 
 13437  nonimmigrant's program. The Regulatory Impact Analysis does model 
 13438  nonimmigrants who would apply for multiple EOS requests across the 10-
 13439  year timeframe, which make up the estimate for the number of EOS 
 13440  requests per year.
 13441      DHS expects foreign students to consider the cost of extending 
 13442  their status in the context of the overall cost of their program, which 
 13443  may include expenses such as tuition, textbooks, room and board, and 
 13444  discretionary expenses. Because the cost of status extension is small, 
 13445  relative to the overall cost of attendance, DHS does not expect this 
 13446  added cost to impose a significant change in burden for foreign 
 13447  students.
 13448      Comments: Commenters stated that the proposed rule fails to account 
 13449  for the costs associated with foreign students and exchange visitors 
 13450  obtaining legal representation. They emphasized that DSOs and ROs are 
 13451  not authorized to provide legal advice, meaning that many foreign 
 13452  students and exchange visitors would need to hire legal counsel to 
 13453  ensure proper completion of filings. Commenters provided alternative 
 13454  cost estimates for legal support when filing an EOS, ranging from $750 
 13455  to $3,000. One of these commenters argued that the EOS filing costs 
 13456  could create
 13457  
 13458  [[Page 45083]]
 13459  
 13460  financial barriers to program completion, specifically referencing 
 13461  doctoral students, who typically earn $30,000 annually.
 13462      Response: DHS acknowledges that nonimmigrants may require legal 
 13463  help in completing the EOS request. This cost is accounted for in the 
 13464  Regulatory Impact Analysis of the NPRM as an average cost of $490, 
 13465  according to the Supporting Statement of Form I-539. As not all 
 13466  nonimmigrants will require legal support, this cost is only applied to 
 13467  24.5 percent \275\ of the nonimmigrants expected to file an EOS request 
 13468  and require additional assistance.
 13469  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 13470  
 13471      \275\ Based on Supporting Statement for Form I-539 values, 24.5 
 13472  percent of F-1, J-1, and I applicants (70% paper applicants * 35% 
 13473  requiring outside assistance = 24.5%) will incur these costs.
 13474  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 13475  
 13476      Comments: One commenter criticized the cost analysis for the 
 13477  biometrics appointments required as part of the EOS process. The 
 13478  commenter specifically noted (1) the use of a ``50 mile round-trip'' 
 13479  without any analysis of the geographic distribution of ASCs in relation 
 13480  to universities (particularly for rural institutions) and (2) the 
 13481  assumption of universal car ownership, ignoring students who rely on 
 13482  public transportation, rideshare services, or who may need to arrange 
 13483  overnight accommodations due to the distance. These oversights, the 
 13484  commenter stated, result in a systematic underestimation of actual 
 13485  costs, which are likely to far exceed DHS's projections. Another 
 13486  commenter stated that biometrics appointments pose a substantial 
 13487  challenge for the majority of foreign students, who frequently lack 
 13488  access to personal transportation.
 13489      Response: DHS disagrees that the cost analysis for the biometrics 
 13490  is underestimated and does not expect this burden to be a significant 
 13491  deterrent to most foreign students. DHS acknowledges that nonimmigrants 
 13492  will incur different travel costs based on location and availability of 
 13493  transportation; they were included in the regulatory impact analysis of 
 13494  the NPRM. The usage of 50 miles is an average distance and is not the 
 13495  same experience for all nonimmigrants. Some will incur small costs due 
 13496  to proximity and low-cost transportation, and others will incur higher 
 13497  costs. This figure is meant to provide an average per nonimmigrant but 
 13498  will not be the specific cost for all nonimmigrants.
 13499  (2) Obtaining an EOS at a POE
 13500      Comments: One commenter remarked that, given the financial burden 
 13501  and uncertainty associated with international travel, exiting and 
 13502  reentering the United States at a POE would not be a viable alternative 
 13503  to filing Form I-539 with USCIS for extending status. The commenter 
 13504  also stated that F-1 and J-1 visa holders, particularly individuals 
 13505  holding single-entry visas, may need to obtain a new visa stamp to 
 13506  travel abroad and reenter the country to extend their period of 
 13507  admission. This may force individuals to remain outside the United 
 13508  States for an extended period of time and impose significant personal 
 13509  cost and risk.
 13510      Response: DHS acknowledges that travelling outside of the United 
 13511  States and re-entering may not be the preferred option for all impacted 
 13512  visa holders. The exact proportion of eligible nonimmigrants who will 
 13513  choose to re-enter through a POE is unknown, but in the regulatory 
 13514  impact analysis for the NPRM and Final Rule, DHS assumes that, while 
 13515  requesting an EOS at a POE is an option, many nonimmigrants wishing to 
 13516  remain in the country will file an EOS and remain in country instead of 
 13517  incurring costs due to travel and reentry. The regulatory impact 
 13518  analysis also assesses how the impacts would change if nonimmigrants 
 13519  sought extensions while traveling through a POE instead of filing the 
 13520  I-539 or I-539A form.
 13521  (3) Unquantifiable and Intangible Costs
 13522      Comments: One commenter stated that DHS does not acknowledge the 
 13523  unquantifiable and intangible costs associated with the uncertainty of 
 13524  applying for a new period of admission. These include (1) the lack of 
 13525  published adjudication data for Form I-539 to inform the likelihood of 
 13526  EOS denial under the proposed rule, (2) current processing time issues 
 13527  at the USCIS California Service Center, which reports an average of 4.5 
 13528  months for changes to F-1 or J-1 status and 3.5 months for extensions, 
 13529  and (3) the inability of applicants to depart the United States after 
 13530  filing an EOS application for fear of abandoning the application and 
 13531  losing their money.
 13532      Response: DHS acknowledges that a denial of EOS may cause an 
 13533  interruption in a student's studies. However, any such denial would be 
 13534  warranted due to an applicant's lack of eligibility for an EOS (i.e., 
 13535  the student is placed on academic probation or suspension, repeatedly 
 13536  fails classes, failed to maintain their nonimmigrant status, or has a 
 13537  criminal history).
 13538      DHS acknowledges backlogs in the processing of EOS applications 
 13539  have occurred due to various factors not related to this rulemaking. 
 13540  DHS believes that factors contributing to this backlog will not be 
 13541  present when more significant influx of EOS applications resulting from 
 13542  this final rule are anticipated to be filed with USCIS. USCIS, as a fee 
 13543  funded agency, may set fees to support the additional workload 
 13544  associated with adjudication of cases subject to section 212(a)(4) of 
 13545  the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(4). USCIS conducts comprehensive fee studies 
 13546  on a biennial basis to assess whether its fee schedule adequately 
 13547  accounts for the full cost of naturalization and adjudication services. 
 13548  This assessment necessarily takes into account the projected volume of 
 13549  filings and the level of effort necessary to adjudicate various 
 13550  immigration benefit requests.\276\ USCIS will allocate appropriate 
 13551  levels of resources to ensure the adjudication of EOS continues in a 
 13552  timely fashion. Due to the expected growth of fees paid for the I-539 
 13553  form, USCIS will have more resources to allocate to meet the demand.
 13554  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 13555  
 13556      \276\ USCIS published a rule to change its fee schedule. See 
 13557  USCIS Fee Schedule and Changes to Certain Other Immigration Benefit 
 13558  Request Requirements, 85 FR 46788 (Aug. 3, 2020), corrected by USCIS 
 13559  Fee Schedule and Changes to Certain Other Immigration Benefit 
 13560  Request Requirements, 85 FR 49941 (Aug. 17, 2020) (Fee Rule). The 
 13561  U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California has 
 13562  preliminarily enjoined DHS from implementing or enforcing any part

 13564  et al., Case No. 20-cv-05883-JSW (N.D. Cal. Sept. 29, 2020). While 
 13565  the Fee Rule is enjoined, USCIS will continue to accept USCIS forms 
 13566  with the current editions and current fees and use the regulations 
 13567  and guidance currently in place to adjudicate applications and 
 13568  petitions.

[2026-14439: lines 17601-17900 of 19533, FR page 45115]
 17601  A. Executive Order 12866: Regulatory Review
 17602  
 17603      Executive Orders 12866 (Regulatory Planning and Review), and 13563 
 17604  (Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review), direct agencies to assess 
 17605  the costs and benefits of available regulatory alternatives and, if 
 17606  regulation is necessary, to select regulatory approaches that maximize 
 17607  net benefits. Executive Order 13563 emphasizes the importance of 
 17608  quantifying both costs and benefits, of reducing costs, harmonizing 
 17609  rules, and promoting flexibility. Executive Order 14192 (Unleashing 
 17610  Prosperity Through Deregulation) directs agencies to significantly 
 17611  reduce the private expenditures required to comply with Federal 
 17612  regulations and provides that ``any new incremental costs associated 
 17613  with new regulations shall, to the extent permitted by law, be offset 
 17614  by the elimination of existing costs associated with at least 10 prior 
 17615  regulations.''
 17616      This rule has been designated a ``significant regulatory action'' 
 17617  that is economically significant under section 3(f)(1) of Executive 
 17618  Order 12866. Accordingly, the rule has been reviewed by the Office of 
 17619  Management and Budget.
 17620      This rule is not an Executive Order 14192 regulatory action because 
 17621  it is being issued with respect to an immigration-related function of 
 17622  the United States. The rule's primary direct purpose is to implement or 
 17623  interpret the immigration laws of the United States (as described in 
 17624  INA 101(a)(17), 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(17)) or any other function performed 
 17625  by the U.S. Federal Government with respect to aliens. See OMB 
 17626  Memorandum M-25-20, ``Guidance Implementing Section 3 of Executive 
 17627  Order 14192, titled `Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation' '' 
 17628  (Mar. 26, 2025).
 17629      DHS provides a summary of the Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA) of 
 17630  the economic impacts below. For the full
 17631  
 17632  [[Page 45116]]
 17633  
 17634  analysis, please see the RIA posted in the docket of this rule on 
 17635  regulations.gov.
 17636      Under the final rule changes, DHS would more frequently have 
 17637  opportunities to review and collect nonimmigrant information, enhancing 
 17638  the Government's oversight and monitoring of these aliens, resulting in 
 17639  costs and benefits. Over a 10-year period of analysis, DHS estimates 
 17640  the final rule would have annualized costs ranging from $443.1 million 
 17641  to $448.6 million (using 3 and 7 percent discount rates, respectively) 
 17642  when considering both U.S. and non-U.S. parties. When considering U.S. 
 17643  parties only, DHS estimates that annualized costs would range from 
 17644  $119.9 million to $125.1 million (using 3 and 7 percent discount rates, 
 17645  respectively).
 17646  Need for the Rule
 17647      The final rule would ensure an effective mechanism for DHS to 
 17648  periodically and directly assess whether these nonimmigrants are 
 17649  complying with the conditions of their classifications and U.S. 
 17650  immigration laws, as well as allow DHS to obtain timely and accurate 
 17651  information about the activities they have engaged in and plan to 
 17652  engage in during their temporary stay in the United States. The 
 17653  opportunity to assess the nonimmigrant status with timely and accurate 
 17654  information allows immigration officers to verify that the 
 17655  nonimmigrants have not obtained any criminal convictions and do not 
 17656  pose a threat to national security. In addition, as F, J, and I 
 17657  nonimmigrants would be admitted for a fixed period of admission under 
 17658  the final rule, they would generally begin to accrue unlawful presence 
 17659  following the expiration of their authorized period of admission, as 
 17660  noted on the Form I-94 (Arrival/Departure Record issued at the POE, and 
 17661  could potentially become inadmissible based on that accrual of unlawful 
 17662  presence under INA section 212(a)(9)(B) and (C), 8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(9)(B) 
 17663  and (C), upon departing the United States. These grounds of 
 17664  inadmissibility have important and far-reaching implications on an 
 17665  alien's future eligibility for a nonimmigrant or immigrant visa, 
 17666  admission to the United States, or adjustment of status to that of a 
 17667  lawful permanent resident. Therefore, these regulatory changes may 
 17668  deter F, J, and I nonimmigrants from failing to maintain status and 
 17669  deter them from engaging in fraud and abuse. By increasing DHS 
 17670  assessments and clarifying when unlawful presence accrual begins, the 
 17671  final rule would strengthen the integrity of these nonimmigrant 
 17672  classifications.
 17673  Affected Population
 17674      The final rule would impact F, J, and I nonimmigrants, DSOs and ROs 
 17675  from SEVP-certified schools and exchange visitor sponsors that run a 
 17676  SEVP- or DoS-designated program and foreign media representatives. 
 17677  Overall, approximately 2.1 million persons participated annually in the 
 17678  F, J, and I nonimmigrant programs combined. DHS estimated the 3-year 
 17679  average active nonimmigrants based on data from fiscal years 2022 to 
 17680  2024. Active nonimmigrants are those present in the United States with 
 17681  a valid visa. Over the 3-year period, there were approximately 1.6 
 17682  million F nonimmigrants, 504,000 J nonimmigrants, and 24,000 I 
 17683  nonimmigrants active per year.
 17684      The number of nonimmigrant EOS requests under the proposed rule 
 17685  depends on the unique circumstances of each nonimmigrant visa holder. 
 17686  For example, in situations when the nonimmigrant intends to extend 
 17687  their stay in the United States in furtherance of their academic 
 17688  training and following the proposed regulatory criteria for their visa 
 17689  and program, they would be expected to file an EOS. Therefore, DHS 
 17690  estimates the number of EOS requests over the 10-year analysis period 
 17691  based on the historical nonimmigrant data and criteria from the 
 17692  proposed regulatory provisions. Further, DHS accounts for the proposed 
 17693  transition period in the estimated number of EOS requests. DHS utilized 
 17694  event-based data to have more accurate estimations of the probability 
 17695  that nonimmigrants would take certain actions that require an EOS 
 17696  request. This allowed DHS to estimate the number of EOS requests based 
 17697  on how nonimmigrants act during their stay. Based on the historical 
 17698  data, regulatory criteria, and the transition period assumptions, DHS 
 17699  estimates an annual average of 393,500; 28,000; 6,000 EOS requests for 
 17700  F, J, and I nonimmigrants, respectively, over the ten-year period of 
 17701  analysis.
 17702  Costs
 17703      DHS recognizes that the final rule would incur costs. Some of the 
 17704  costs have been quantified based on available data, and the remaining 
 17705  costs are qualitative.
 17706  Quantitative Costs
 17707      Depending on each nonimmigrant's need to extend his or her stay in 
 17708  the United States, nonimmigrants on an F-1, F-2, J-1, J-2 and I visa 
 17709  would incur costs to request an EOS. The cost burden includes 
 17710  application fees and time for filing Form I-539 or I-539A. DHS assumes 
 17711  a percentage of nonimmigrants would incur costs for additional help 
 17712  filing their request for EOS. DHS estimates the annualized EOS costs 
 17713  for the nonimmigrants would range from $317.9 million to $317.3 million 
 17714  (using 3 and 7 percent discount rates, respectively).
 17715      DHS also calculated a familiarization cost for nonimmigrants 
 17716  expected to be in the country when the rule goes into effect. This 1 
 17717  hour of burden, which is an advising burden to meet with their DSOs and 
 17718  ROs, resulted in an additional year 1 cost of $45.6 million to $43.9 
 17719  million (using 3 and 7 percent discount rates, respectively).
 17720      Further, DSOs and ROs would incur a burden for assisting additional 
 17721  EOS requests resulting from this final rule. When a nonimmigrant is or 
 17722  would be employed under OPT or CPT, DHS assumes HR staff would incur 
 17723  burden per EOS request to track form updates and avoid inadvertent 
 17724  unauthorized employment due to form discrepancies with the Form I-9. 
 17725  DHS estimates the annualized EOS costs for the DSOs and ROs, and HR 
 17726  staff would range from $88.5 million to $88.3 million (using 3 and 7 
 17727  percent discount rates, respectively).
 17728      Additionally, DHS assumes DSOs and ROs would incur costs to 
 17729  familiarize themselves with the rule and to create and modify training 
 17730  materials, and other adaptations such as system wide briefings, 
 17731  systemic changes, and advising of current nonimmigrants of the rule 
 17732  changes. For the final rule, DHS updated the familiarization costs to 
 17733  135 hours per DSO and RO based on public comments received. DHS also 
 17734  added 1 hour of advising burden to DSO, ROs and current nonimmigrants 
 17735  subject to this rule to account for the transition between the old and 
 17736  new rule. The 1 hour advising burden to nonimmigrants resulted in an 
 17737  additional cost of $45.6 million to $43.9 million (using 3 and 7 
 17738  percent discount rates, respectively). DHS estimates the 
 17739  familiarization and adaptation and advising costs in year 1 to DSOs and 
 17740  ROs would range from $267.9 million to $257.8 million (using 3 and 7 
 17741  percent discount rates, respectively).
 17742  Qualitative Costs
 17743      DHS acknowledges there could be other costs that the Department was 
 17744  not able to quantify and discusses these in the following section. 
 17745  Generally, DHS lacked data and information to quantify the qualitative 
 17746  costs below.
 17747  Federal Government Costs
 17748      DHS acknowledges there will be implementation and operational costs 
 17749  to the government associated with
 17750  
 17751  [[Page 45117]]
 17752  
 17753  assessing aliens at the POE for purposes of authorizing an admission 
 17754  period of up to 4 years. CBP officers will need training on new systems

  6403      Comments: Many commenters expressed concerns that the proposed EOS

  6413  class offerings and modality, and full-time enrollment requisites, and 
  6414  requiring extensions would be burdensome for such students. Concerns 
  6415  were raised about USCIS's capacity to process EOS applications in a 
  6416  timely manner, risking delays or administrative errors that could 
  6417  result in students unintentionally falling out of status.
  6418      Commenters urged DHS to consider the practical challenges and time 
  6419  constraints associated with the EOS process, noting that existing 
  6420  oversight through SEVIS, DSO reports, and DHS monitoring is already 
  6421  robust. They also highlighted that the proposed requirements do not 
  6422  account for the variety of academic scenarios, such as the needs of 
  6423  English language students, those in short-term programs, or students in
